prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: In opening I ranked topological insulators (B010) first, and I still regard it as a genuine new class of quantum matter with a textbook theory-experiment story. But the opening ballots show that optical lattice clocks (B001) carry the strongest and most scientifically argued support: four first places, six top-three rankings, and consistent two-name attribution (Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realisation, Ye for taking it to 10^-18 and the many-body clock physics). What persuades me is exactly what I look for in a prize: a result that is quantitative, independently reproduced by several laboratories that now compare clocks across continents, and fully understood from atomic theory, including the systematic shifts. Its consequences (relativistic geodesy, tests of time dilation over millimetres, searches for varying constants and dark matter, the pending redefinition of the second) are concrete and checkable. Quantum mechanics, a century on, still gives us the most precise measurements humans have ever made. The attribution is also cleaner than for any condensed-matter candidate on the shortlist, where the three-person cap forces cuts that leave out strong claimants.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one Ulf Danielsson and Eva Olsson raise: lattice clocks may be read as a refinement of the frequency-comb (2005) and trapped-ion clock (2012) prizes rather than a new discovery, and other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, the PTB and NIST clocks) have claims the two-name credit cannot cover. There is also a timing argument for waiting until the SI second is redefined. As a condensed-matter physicist I am further conscious that I am setting aside a field in which I have deeper expertise, and that this shift could reflect a wish for consensus more than my own judgment of merit; I have tried to guard against that by asking whether B001 would be my choice if the vote counts were hidden. On the science and the attribution, I conclude it is a defensible first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first as a concrete, nature-checkable instrument result, but flags the worry that the committee may regard it as a technological refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 clock prizes, and that other clock groups could be argued as comparably decisive.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously, but I do not think it holds. The comb prize rewarded the frequency-measurement tool and the 2012 prize rewarded single-ion control; the magic-wavelength trapping of thousands of neutral atoms, cancelling the light shift, is a distinct physical idea that changes the statistical power of the measurement and opens many-body clock physics, with the 10^-18 level reached only that way. I agree on the other groups: the credit is not unique, but Katori's priority on the concept and Ye's on the record performance make the pair defensible, and I would want the citation to say 'optical lattice clocks' rather than precision measurement in general.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B001 first as precision atomic physics she trusts, but she also ranks B010 seventh, says condensed matter is outside her main expertise, and notes the 2016 topological-phase prize and unresolved credit among Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Molenkamp.
responses.response: Your caution on B010 is fair, and it is the main reason I am moving off my own first choice. The credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan is genuinely split, Zhang is no longer available, and the three-person cap forces cuts I cannot defend as cleanly as Katori and Ye. I would add that, from the inside, the 2016 prize recognised topological phases and the quantum Hall-type invariants, not time-reversal-invariant materials, so B010 is not duplicative; that is why I keep it as an alternative rather than dropping it. On B001 I appreciate your point that you have not verified every priority detail, and I would ask you to say which claims about Lemonde or Ludlow you would want checked before the citation is fixed.

responses.point: Mehlig puts the 2D melting theory (B006) first for its simple, universal defect-unbinding mechanism, ranks the lattice clocks second, and judges magic-angle graphene (B017) probably premature because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with you on B017: the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity is solid and highly replicated, but the pairing mechanism is open and the field is about seven years old, which is why I demote it from my second place to an alternative. On B006 I respect the elegance, and as a theorist I like the mechanism, but I share your own reservation that the evidence is system-dependent and that some melting transitions are first order, and that it builds on the Kosterlitz-Thouless work already honoured in 2016. With only you supporting it in opening, I do not see it as the strongest case this year; I would be interested in whether you would accept B001 as a second-best on the merits.

responses.point: Olsson ranks room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance (B015) first as an original discovery with decisive technological impact, a successor to the 2007 GMR prize, and ranks the clocks second while asking whether they are a refinement of earlier prizes.
responses.response: I ranked B015 third myself and value the same thing you do, a clear spin-dependent tunnelling effect that is explained by band-structure theory for epitaxial MgO. My reservation is attribution: the 1995 Miyazaki and Moodera result and the MgO step are different discoveries, Parkin's role in the MgO step is shared with the Yuasa and Djayaprawira groups who are not credited, and Julliere's 1975 precursor complicates priority. A prize built on this would need to settle which discovery is being honoured, and I do not think that is settled. The closeness to GMR is also a real concern, though not decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee considers optical lattice clocks sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes, or would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the SI second.
Whether the contributions of other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others) should reduce or reshape the Katori and Ye credit.
For my alternative B010, how to divide credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal under a three-person cap.
Whether the pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene will be clarified soon enough to remove the maturity objection to B017.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B001, B010 or B017. I note only general scientific proximity to the condensed-matter candidates (topological insulators and moire materials), where my group uses first-principles electronic-structure methods, and I do not collaborate with any credited person that I know of from the profile.
